title: The Philosopher's Scroll: Classical Arguments
welcome_lead: Step into the cloistered library where Aquinas, Anselm, and Paley still argue across the centuries about the existence of God.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on classical arguments for God's existence: cosmological, teleological, and ontological.
final_note: You have traced the great classical arguments. Carry the questions, not just the answers.

An a posteriori argument from the apparent design or purpose in nature to a designer, classically presented by William Paley.
An a priori argument from the concept of God as the greatest conceivable being to His necessary existence, originating with Anselm.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In the Summa Theologica (1265-1274), Thomas Aquinas presents five proofs (quinque viae) for God's existence. The first three are cosmological: from motion, from causation, and from contingency. The fourth is from gradation (degrees of perfection) and the fifth is teleological (from governance of things).

Each argument concludes 'and this everyone understands to be God', linking philosophical reasoning to the God of classical theism.

William Paley's Natural Theology (1802) opens with the famous analogy: if one finds a watch on a heath, its intricate parts arranged for a purpose point inevitably to a watchmaker. Likewise, the complexity of the natural world points to a divine designer.

Paley extends this to the eye, the heart, and the heavens, arguing that order and adaptation cannot arise by chance.

In the Proslogion (1078), Anselm defines God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived'. He argues that if God existed only in the understanding, a greater being (existing in reality also) could be conceived, which is a contradiction.

Therefore God must exist in reality as well as in the mind. Gaunilo famously responded with his 'Lost Island' parody.

mcqs.q: Whose work contains the Five Ways?
options: Thomas Aquinas
William Paley
Anselm of Canterbury
David Hume

mcqs.q: Paley's watchmaker analogy is an example of which type of argument?
options: Teleological
Ontological
Cosmological
Moral
Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.
The ontological argument is the same as the cosmological argument.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.

mcqs.q: What does the cosmological argument try to prove?
options: That the existence of the universe requires a first cause or necessary being — usually identified with God — to explain why anything exists at all.
The ontological argument is the same as the cosmological argument.
The cosmological argument proves the Big Bang happened.
The cosmological argument proves who created life on Earth.

mcqs.q: What is distinctive about the ontological argument?
options: It tries to prove God's existence purely from the concept of God — a priori reasoning needing no empirical evidence about the world.
The cosmological argument proves the Big Bang happened.
The ontological argument uses scientific evidence to prove God exists.
The ontological argument is the same as the cosmological argument.

mcqs.q: In what year was Anselm's Proslogion written?
Paley pointed to the eye as evidence of design because:
options: its intricate adaptation to the purpose of seeing parallels the contrivance of a designed instrument
the eye is the only organ science cannot explain
the eye proves the universe had a beginning
the eye demonstrates necessary existence

mcqs.q: Hume argues that, at most, the design argument proves:
options: a cause proportioned to the finite effect — not an infinite, perfect creator
the God of classical theism exactly
that no designer of any kind exists
that design is logically impossible

mcqs.q: The difference between Anselm's two forms of the ontological argument is that the second argues God:
options: has necessary existence — God cannot even be conceived not to exist
exists in the understanding alone
is the first cause of motion
is probable rather than certain

mcqs.q: Aquinas rejected the ontological argument because:
options: humans cannot know God's essence in this life, so cannot argue from it to his existence
he denied that God exists necessarily
he thought all arguments for God fail
Gaunilo had refuted it conclusively
